content: For iid Bernoulli trials with success probability p, what is the cleanest exact method for finding the probability of at least one streak of k successes in n trials? I would use a finite-state recurrence, though a Poisson approximation seems tempting when such streaks are rare.

A finite-state recurrence is the clean exact method. Track the current trailing run length from zero through k minus one, then update those state probabilities after each trial; entering state k records that a qualifying streak has occurred. Equivalently, compute the probability of never reaching k and subtract from one. A Poisson approximation can work in a rare-streak regime, but overlapping candidate windows make a naive count inaccurate.

How should the recurrence change if I need the number of maximal success runs rather than merely the occurrence of a length-k substring? Boundary runs seem to need separate treatment, and runs longer than k should count once rather than through all their overlapping windows.

Then the state should retain enough information to recognize when a run ends. Track the current success-run length, capped if only thresholds matter, and increment the count when a failure closes a qualifying run. At the final boundary, close any still-open run explicitly. A run of length greater than k then contributes once. If you need the full count distribution, attach a count index or use a probability-generating function.

I used “streak of k” imprecisely earlier: an exact maximal run of length k differs from a run of at least k. Is there a useful limiting approximation for maximal runs, or does clumping make the finite-state calculation preferable except in carefully scaled regimes?

Clumping is the central issue. In rare-event limits, starts of maximal qualifying runs can often be approximated by a Poisson process because requiring a preceding failure removes much of the overlap. The rate is roughly based on patterns such as failure followed by k successes, with boundary corrections. For moderate n, common p, or exact-length runs, the dependence between nearby patterns remains material, so the finite-state calculation is safer.
After six heads in a row, I think tails has to be more likely next because the results need to balance out. What is independence supposed to mean if a long run can keep making the totals more uneven?

Independence means the previous outcomes do not change the probability of the next one. For a fair coin, tails remains one half after six heads. Balance is a long-run tendency, not a force correcting short-run totals. As more flips accumulate, the existing difference usually becomes small relative to the total number of flips, even though the coin never actively compensates for a streak.

But ten heads in a row and a mixed ten-flip string like heads, tails, heads, tails, and so on have the same exact chance. Does that mean streaks are not unusual at all, and people only notice them because the pattern looks simpler?

Each particular ten-flip sequence has probability one in 1,024, so those two exact sequences are equally likely. The difference is that “mixed” describes many possible sequences, while “ten heads” describes only one. Long streaks can therefore be unusual as a category even though no individual irregular-looking sequence is more likely than that particular streak. Human attention to simple patterns adds another layer, but the grouping already explains the probability difference.
What is the chance of getting some run if I toss a coin many times? I am vague about whether I should multiply the chances for one chosen block or add up every place where the run could appear.

For one chosen block of k fair-coin flips, an all-heads run has probability 2 to the power of minus k. Across many possible starting places, simply adding those probabilities double-counts outcomes containing overlapping runs. The reliable approach is the recurrence described earlier: track how many consecutive heads currently trail the sequence and compute the chance of avoiding k until the final toss, then subtract that chance from one.

Suppose trials are conditionally independent given an unknown Bernoulli parameter, but p itself varies across coins. Marginally, outcomes from the same coin are exchangeable rather than independent. Is posterior predictive covariance the most direct way to quantify the apparent clustering of successes?

Yes. Conditional on p, two outcomes have zero covariance, but after integrating over uncertainty in p, their covariance is the variance of p. Observing a success shifts posterior mass toward larger p, raising the predictive chance of another success. That produces clustering without any time-varying mechanism. The same distinction matters for streaks: conditional calculations use a fixed p, whereas marginal calculations average streak probabilities over the distribution of p.

Does the dependence vanish asymptotically as observations identify each coin’s p, or only in the posterior predictive distribution conditional on a sufficiently long history? Across newly sampled coins, I would expect the mixture-induced correlation to persist because heterogeneity has not disappeared.

That distinction is right. For one repeatedly observed coin, posterior uncertainty about its p typically contracts, so predictive dependence caused solely by uncertainty becomes small. Across newly sampled coins, population heterogeneity remains: two outcomes from the same new coin share a latent p and stay positively correlated marginally. Outcomes from independently sampled coins need not share that covariance, assuming their latent parameters are independent draws.

I should separate epistemic dependence from physical dependence: integrating out p couples predictions, but it does not make one flip causally affect the next. Can finite binary data distinguish stable between-coin heterogeneity from genuine within-coin state persistence without stronger design assumptions?

Usually not cleanly. Both latent heterogeneity and state persistence can create excess runs and positive serial association. Repeated sequences from many labeled coins help: heterogeneity predicts stable coin-specific rates, while a state model predicts dependence on recent outcomes after accounting for those rates. Even then, short sequences can leave the mechanisms weakly identified. Interventions, randomized coin changes, or well-specified hierarchical and Markov models provide stronger separation.

I think flips from the same coin are independent no matter what, because one toss cannot touch the next toss. Why does merely not knowing whether the coin is good or bad make the results connected in the calculation?

The tosses may be physically independent once that coin’s fixed bias is specified. Your predictions are connected because they share the same unknown bias. A first head is evidence that this coin may favor heads, so it changes what you should predict for the second toss. Nothing travels from one toss to the next; both outcomes carry information about one common, hidden property.

If a coin gives four heads together, that proves something has shifted and another head is now the safer guess. A fair coin would spread the heads around instead of putting them all next to each other, wouldn't it?

Four heads are evidence against fairness only to a limited degree; they do not prove a shift, and fair coins naturally produce clusters. If the coin’s bias is truly fixed but unknown, the run can raise your estimated probability of heads. If the coin is known to be fair and tosses are independent, the next probability remains one half. The interpretation depends on which assumption is uncertain, not on the run alone.
What is the simple way to tell whether a streak came from a lopsided coin or just happened? I would count the heads, but I do not see why their order matters if the total is the same.

If the only alternative is a fixed bias, the total number of heads contains the relevant information; order adds nothing. Order matters when the alternative involves changing behavior, such as a coin whose probability drifts or depends on the previous result. Then compare both the total and transition patterns, ideally across a much longer sequence. With little data, a streak rarely distinguishes these explanations confidently.

For a specified binary pattern such as HHTH, the expected waiting time depends on self-overlap rather than only on its probability. Is a prefix-suffix automaton the most transparent derivation, especially when comparing a pattern with a pure streak like HHHH?

Yes. Use states representing the longest suffix observed so far that is also a prefix of the target pattern. First-step equations from those states give the expected remaining waiting time. Self-overlap matters because a mismatch may preserve partial progress. For a fair coin, HHTH overlaps only at its one-symbol border, while HHHH overlaps at several lengths; that makes the pure streak take longer on average than its one-block probability suggests.

Would the same automaton yield the entire waiting-time distribution by attaching a transition matrix and treating completion as absorbing? I suspect the tail behavior is governed by the largest subunit eigenvalue, although finite-horizon probabilities may still require careful initialization.

Exactly. Build the transient-state transition matrix Q and an absorbing completion state. Starting from the empty-prefix vector, the probability of still waiting after n trials is obtained from Q raised to the nth power. The dominant eigenvalue of Q controls the asymptotic geometric tail when the chain is irreducible on its transient states. Initialization and indexing matter for exact finite horizons, particularly when the pattern could finish on the final trial.

I should sharpen the contrast: HHTH has a length-one border because both its prefix and suffix are H, whereas HHHH has several borders. Does the standard mean formula add powers of the alphabet size corresponding to every border, including the full pattern?

Correct. For an equiprobable alphabet, the expected waiting time is the sum of alphabet-size powers for all border lengths, including the full pattern length. Thus a fair-coin pattern contributes 2 raised to each relevant border length. HHTH has border lengths one and four, giving 2 plus 16, while HHHH has borders one, two, three, and four, giving 2 plus 4 plus 8 plus 16.

If four heads has chance one in sixteen, then it must turn up once every sixteen tosses. I think that means a run missing from the first fifteen tosses is basically due on the sixteenth. Why isn't that right?

One in sixteen is the chance that one specified block of four tosses is all heads, not a schedule for appearances. Overlapping blocks share tosses, and failures can erase different amounts of partial progress. For HHHH, the expected wait from a fresh start is actually thirty tosses. Even an unusually long wait does not make completion due at a fixed time; only the current trailing heads affect the immediate chance of finishing.

After three heads, another head would complete a very rare group, so tails should be much more likely at that point. Does the coin somehow restart after tails, while heads has to fight against the rarity of the whole group?

For independent fair tosses, the next result remains equally likely to be heads or tails. The rarity of four consecutive heads describes the whole four-toss event before those tosses occur. Once three heads are already known, only one uncertain toss remains, and it has probability one half of completing the run. A tail resets progress toward HHHH, but it is not made more likely by doing so.

What does an average wait of thirty really mean if the streak can happen on toss four or not for hundreds of tosses? I picture an average as the usual spot, but this one sounds too spread out for that.

The mean is the long-run average waiting time across many fresh repetitions; it need not be the most common or typical waiting time. Waiting distributions are right-skewed: completion can occur quickly, while a small fraction of very long waits pulls the mean upward. A median answers a different question—the point by which half of repetitions have finished—and can be substantially below the mean.

Under a null model of independent games with heterogeneous win probabilities p_i, how would you approximate the distribution of the longest winning streak? Treating games as identically distributed seems untenable when opponent strength and venue vary, but conditioning on the full schedule may be computationally awkward.

Condition on the scheduled probabilities and use a dynamic program whose state is the current run length and the largest run seen. Each game updates those states with its own p_i. That gives an exact conditional distribution without assuming identical games. For a quicker approximation, simulation from the scheduled probabilities is straightforward. The result is only as credible as the p_i estimates, so parameter uncertainty should also be propagated when material.

If the reported streak is selected after scanning many teams and seasons, should the reference distribution maximize over that entire search set? I assume evaluating only the highlighted team's fixed window would severely understate the chance of seeing some comparable extreme.

Yes. The null comparison should reproduce the selection procedure that produced the claim. Simulate or calculate the maximum streak across the same teams, seasons, and eligible windows, including any rules used to highlight it. Testing only the chosen sequence answers a narrower, pre-specified question and incurs selection bias. Dependence between teams or overlapping seasons may complicate the calculation, making joint simulation especially useful.

I should qualify independence here: schedule-adjusted Bernoulli trials can still miss serial dependence from fatigue or lineup changes. For a hot-state alternative, would a hidden Markov model be more identifiable than adding the previous outcome to a logistic regression, or merely more flexible and assumption-heavy?

A hidden Markov model is more flexible, not automatically more identifiable. It can represent persistent latent states, but state-transition rates and state-specific success probabilities may be weakly determined by ordinary win-loss sequences. Lagged logistic regression is easier to interpret, yet a previous-outcome coefficient can absorb omitted schedule or lineup effects. Rich covariates, long sequences, pre-specified comparisons, and out-of-sample prediction help distinguish genuine persistence from model artifacts.
A player who makes five shots in a row is clearly on a roll, so the sixth shot is more likely to go in. Why call the shots independent when they all come from the same person in the same game?

Independence is a model claim, not something guaranteed by using separate attempts. Under that model, the five makes do not alter the sixth shot's chance once relevant conditions are fixed. In reality, shot difficulty, fatigue, confidence, and defense may vary. A streak alone does not prove a hot state, because independent attempts also cluster. You would compare the next-shot rate after streaks with an appropriate, pre-specified baseline while controlling for those conditions.
If the next shot misses, I think that cancels the streak and shows the earlier makes were just luck. But if it goes in, doesn't that confirm the player really had the hot thing going?

Neither single outcome settles the explanation. A miss can occur during a genuinely higher-probability state, and another make can occur under a constant-probability model. Judging the hypothesis differently after seeing which result occurred also creates a flexible, one-sided story. Evidence for a hot state comes from a pre-defined pattern repeated across enough attempts, with uncertainty and changing shot conditions accounted for.
What is the chance of some player getting a long run, then? Do I multiply one player's shot chance several times, or add something for every player and every stretch where the run might start?

Multiplying gives the probability for one specified player and one specified block, assuming equal independent shot probabilities. Searching every player and starting point creates many chances for a run, and those chances overlap, so simple addition can overcount. A simulation is often easiest: reproduce each player's attempt probabilities, generate whole games repeatedly, and record the longest streak anywhere. The fraction exceeding your target estimates the search-wide probability.
